content.title: About
content.content: Fruit muffin is a small baked good made from wheat flour, eggs, milk and fresh fruit (usually berries or diced apple). It has a soft, slightly moist crumb and a sweet‑tart flavor from the fruit. Muffins are often served as a snack or dessert and are convenient to take on the go.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first muffin recipe appeared in England in the 19th century, and fruit‑filled versions became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Fruit muffins are frequently used as a "grab‑and‑go" breakfast because they pack easily and require no utensils.
There are more than 30 fruit muffin variations: blueberry, strawberry, kiwi, mango and even exotic fruits like dragon fruit.
Traditionally muffins are baked in a special cup‑shaped pan that gives them their characteristic round shape.
In some countries muffins are finished with a light dusting of powdered sugar or a thin glaze.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Fruit muffins provide vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The fruit component adds fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries and other colorful fruits are high in antioxidants (anthocyanins, vitamin C) that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from flour and fruit quickly replenish glucose stores, making muffins a good pre‑workout snack.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from the fruit enhances the body’s immune defenses.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Fruit muffins often contain added sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free versions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter, eggs and sugar, muffins are relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some commercial recipes use margarine that contains trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and topped with cottage cheese, yogurt or nut butter. They are often paired with tea or coffee. A cooled muffin holds its shape, while a gently warmed one releases more aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the microwave or oven before eating to restore softness.
